destination.title: Fifty years later the FBI still cannot name him

short21: He jumped out of a plane with two hundred thousand dollars — and vanished forever.
A calm man in a dark suit, ticketed as Dan Cooper, hijacked a flight from Portland to Seattle with a note claiming he had a bomb.
He demanded two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes, let the passengers go, then ordered the crew to fly low toward Mexico City.
, he lowered the plane's rear stairs and parachuted into a freezing night over Washington.
The FBI chased it for forty-five years — the only unsolved hijacking in U.S.
In 1980 a boy found about fifty-eight hundred dollars of the cash by a river, and the serial numbers matched.
It's the only money ever found.
In 2016 the FBI suspended the case — suspended, not solved.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: On the night before Thanksgiving, in 1971, a quiet man talked his way onto a passenger plane, threatened it with a bomb, collected a fortune in cash, and walked out the back of the aircraft into the dark sky.
The world came to know him by a name that was never even his.
None of it was ever enough to give him a name.
A short hop, Portland to Seattle, the kind of late-afternoon flight nobody is supposed to remember.
He took a seat near the back of the Boeing 727, ordered a drink, and waited.
Cooper ever since, which means that even his fake name is, in a small way, a mistake nobody ever managed to correct.
Whether any of it was real, nobody on that airplane could possibly know, and that uncertainty was the whole weapon.
About thirty-six of them filed off the plane, most of them never quite realizing, until they read about it later, how close they had been to the most famous skyjacking in American history.
None of this happened in a rush, and the patience of it is part of what unnerves people.
He had chosen a Boeing 727 on purpose, and he understood its one unusual feature better than most passengers ever would.
The Boeing 727 carried a set of stairs built into its tail, under the fuselage.
If he came down hurt, or came down in the water, there were a hundred different ways for the wilderness to take him and never give him back.
Nobody knows for certain which chute he strapped on in the dark, or whether the one he chose ever opened.

He hit the trees at speed in the dark, or the cold finished him, or he came down in a river and was swept away, and his body and his money sank into a wilderness so vast that searchers, even knowing roughly where to look, never turned up a trace.
Not a single one of those marked twenty-dollar bills.
Fifty years of investigation has never been able to clearly favor one ending over the other.
The country has never been able to choose, so it kept both.
There was no photograph, because in 1971 there was no camera pointed at a man in seat eighteen-E.

Fly toward Mexico City. Stay low, under ten thousand feet. Keep the speed down, the wing flaps lowered, the landing gear hanging in the wind. And leave the rear staircase, the aft airstair, unlocked.
